papers.title: SKAD: Sketch-Guided Audio-Contrastive Decoding for Reasoning in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have shown increasing potential in audio understanding and reasoning by generating intermediate reasoning steps before answering. However, directly eliciting long-form reasoning from audio does not always lead to more reliable predictions. Even reasoning-oriented LALMs may gradually shift from acoustic evidence to language-continuation patterns during generation. A natural solution is to use contrastive decoding with an audio-masked branch, but directly applying this strategy to plain chain-of-thought reasoning is often ineffective, since the masked branch lacks sufficient audio-related context and provides an unstable reference. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SKAD} (\textbf{Sk}etch-Guided \textbf{A}udio-Contrastive \textbf{D}ecoding), a training-free inference-time method for audio reasoning. SKAD first constructs an acoustic evidence sketch that summarizes question-relevant auditory information. It then performs contrastive decoding between an audio-conditioned reasoning branch and a sketch-only branch. By using the sketch as a shared semantic scaffold, SKAD makes the masked branch more informative and encourages decoding decisions that are more dependent on the original audio. We evaluate SKAD on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and Step-Audio-R1 across three audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks: MMAR, MMAU, and MMSU. Experimental results show that SKAD consistently improves the average accuracy of both models across all benchmarks. Further ablations show that direct contrastive decoding without the acoustic evidence sketch provides limited or negative gains, confirming the importance of constructing a reliable contrastive reference before audio-contrastive decoding.

papers.title: Uncovering Audio-Text Alignment in Large Audio-Language Models through Cross-Modal Concept Neurons
papers.abstract: While the language model backbone is pretrained on text alone, large audio-language models (LALMs) can, to a great extent, recognize acoustic attributes, such as emotion, speaker gender, and spoken language. However, it is unclear how the audio representation is integrated, if at all, with the other text representation before the model produces text. We hypothesize that there is a shared subspace where the audio and text representations are aligned. To test this hypothesis, we identify cross-modal neurons that are responsible for representing both audio and text. We find alignment between audio and text neurons to various degrees across three LALMs and four acoustic attribute types. Causal interventions, steering and deactivating the neurons, confirm that the cross-modal neurons are not just necessary for prediction but can also be manipulated.

papers.title: Preference-Aware Pareto Steering for Multi-Task Speech LLMs
papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) perform multiple tasks, including automatic speech recognition (ASR), timestamp prediction (TS), and speech translation (ST). Joint training of speech LLMs creates task trade-offs, yet standard training with fixed loss weights does not generally control the resulting trade-off according to deployment preferences. To address this, we propose Endpoint-Anchored Preference-Aware Sampling Uniformly along the Pareto Front (EA-SURF), an a priori method that adapts scalarization weights so that the resulting task trade-off reflects the desired preference. EA-SURF retains the standard weighted-loss training pipeline, tracking the current model's performance relative to each task-specific reference and adapting the scalarization weights as training proceeds. We theoretically show that EA-SURF can match a desired preference, with the update becoming stationary at the target under checkable regularity conditions. Across six three-objective speech LLM requests, EA-SURF empirically converges toward the requested targets and increases endpoint-inclusive normalized hypervolume by 17.8% over fixed loss weighting.

papers.title: Speech LLMs That Breathe: Modeling Non-Verbal Vocalizations in Dialogue
papers.abstract: The user experience of speech interaction models has improved, benefiting from the modeling of paralinguistic attributes and advances in speech reconstruction paradigms. However, human communication follows extensive norms regarding non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) spanning respiratory, affective, and discourse. The omission of these events imposes inherent limitations on the naturalness of current approaches. In this work, we cover 13 major types of NVVs and construct a natural dialogue dataset that conforms to human conversational norms through an automated synthesis pipeline. We enhance the ability of speech interaction models to generate contextually appropriate NVV events through multi-stage fine-tuning and NVV-aware GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Based on distinct modeling paradigms, we substantially improve the expressiveness of VocalNet and VITA-Qinyu in empathy interactions and role-play dialogues, and further discuss the architectural necessity for achieving high-quality natural speech generation.

papers.title: Steering intonational tunes in text-to-speech synthesis
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech systems built on residual vector quantization often generate audio in two stages: a transformer backbone emits the first level of each frame's token stack, and a smaller depth model generates the rest autoregressively. We ask which components of such a model are responsible for prosodic intonation, more precisely for generating the English nuclear tune (for instance, the falling pitch melody that distinguishes an assertion from a question's rising melody), and whether interventions on those components can be used to control intonation. Prompt-based control mostly fails; only a final question mark is a reliable lever. Interchange interventions in CSM and S2 locate the tune: the backbone's hidden state carries it to the waveform through the depth model, and the first level of the stack carries little or none of it. Steering the backbone state with a difference-of-means vector computed on new material generated with a final period or question mark moves the tune, but the push toward an assertion degrades the voice. Steering vectors computed instead from the backbone states associated with human imitations of theoretically-specified tunes, whose text carries no punctuation, and applied inside the generation loop, move most recordings to the other condition in both systems (even when fitted without the speaker being steered), at a small cost in predicted naturalness. These imitation-derived vectors are aligned with the one obtained from the two punctuated conditions far beyond a shuffled-label null, so the backbone state of a punctuated prompt already represents intonation. The steered recordings broadly become falling or rising, according to the intent, but the edge tone moves more coherently than the pitch accent, and the target tune cannot be selected precisely beyond this broad tendency.

papers.title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
papers.abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.

papers.title: SLM-SS: Token-Based Speech Separation with Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Speech separation (SS) has witnessed substantial progress in recent years with the advent of neural network-based methods, achieving notable improvements on signal-level evaluation metrics. Existing speech separation systems are mostly optimized with signal-level objectives, and often yield outputs that are acceptable in waveform metrics but suboptimal for intelligibility-sensitive downstream tasks. To address this gap, we propose SLM-SS, a token-based generative speech separation framework that models multi-talker mixtures with speech language models. We first discretize clean speech into multi-codebook token sequences with neural codecs and serialize multi-speaker targets via Serialized Output Training (SOT). An encoder-decoder autoregressive speech language model predicts the zero-order sequence to establish speaker ordering and coarse linguistic content, and a non-autoregressive module then refines higher-order residual codebooks for efficient reconstruction. We further introduce a per-talker non-autoregressive strategy that simplifies high-order modeling and improves the stability. On Libri2Mix, SLM-SS with per-talker NAR achieves $6.92\%$ WER, approaching codec-only reconstruction. The WavTokenizer variant eliminates NAR refinement and achieves the highest mean subjective quality score among evaluated separation systems. Its UTMOS and DNSMOS advantages over discriminative baselines persist on unseen noisy and Chinese mixtures without fine-tuning.

papers.title: RealComm: Benchmarking and Adapting Audio Deepfake Detection over Real Communication Channels
papers.abstract: Acoustic capture, device processing, and transmission coding in real calls jointly alter speech signals and may affect the reliability of audio deepfake detection. To systematically evaluate these effects, we introduce RealComm, a dataset pairing digital speech with recordings of the same utterances transmitted through real mobile calls. The acquisition design covers acoustic and wired injection, handset and speakerphone operation, and caller-side denoising, with bona fide and synthetic speech recorded under matched conditions. The dataset includes RealCommBench for evaluation and RealCommTrain for adaptation. We further develop RealComm-Aug, a staged waveform augmentation pipeline for simulating acquisition and transmission effects, and investigate its combination with real-call training. Experiments with existing detectors reveal substantial degradation after call transmission, even for models with strong digital-domain performance; acoustic injection is particularly challenging. Paired quality and spectral analyses show that quality degradation is associated with poorer detection across recording conditions for the evaluated detectors, while high-frequency attenuation alone does not explain detection difficulty. Simulated augmentation and real-call training provide complementary benefits, with their combination achieving the lowest call-domain error for each of three evaluated detectors. For Teffic-Audio, the equal error rate decreases from 37.94% to 22.37%. The demo and benchmark access information are provided through the project repository.

papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.

papers.title: LoCA: Local Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning of Autoregressive Flow-Matching TTS
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning can improve text-to-speech synthesis through feedback on generated speech. However, sentence-level rewards do not identify local errors, while signed regression updates can lead to excessive fitting or repulsion of sampled outputs. We propose LoCA (Local Credit Assignment) for autoregressive flow-matching text-to-speech. LoCA uses ASR-based text alignment to locate content errors in generated speech and redistribute sentence-level advantages across acoustic frames. To improve training stability, we introduce reference-relative positive and negative thresholds that limit continued fitting and repulsion. Experiments on VoxCPM2 show that LoCA reduces sample-weighted content error on a multilingual CV3 evaluation subset by 20.5% and 14.3% relative to the pretrained backbone and GROW, respectively, while improving speaker similarity. LoCA also improves content accuracy on the Seed-TTS-Eval hard subset. Ablation results support the contributions of local credit and threshold-based regression control.

papers.title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
papers.abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.

papers.title: Pronouncing Hard Words: Phoneme Adaptation of a Pretrained Conversational Text to Speech Model
papers.abstract: Voice agents built as cascaded automatic speech recognition (ASR)->large language model (LLM)->text-to-speech (TTS) pipelines increasingly rely on conversational TTS: streaming, context conditioned models that adapt delivery to dialogue history. Such models are natural and expressive but offer little explicit control over how rare, trust-critical drug names are pronounced, because these entities are too infrequent, and their vocabulary too fast-growing, to be covered by any amount of pre-, mid-, or post-training. We retrofit phoneme controllability onto a pretrained conversational TTS model without any pre/mid-training, using an ARPAbet vocabulary exten-sion, continued phoneme-augmented supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a training-free inference-time acoustic-biasing step. On a 7,500 clip clinical drug-pronunciation evaluation, our model raises strict Gemini-judged correctness from 54.6% (no phoneme augmentation) to 90.7%, outperforming every conversational and stateless TTS baseline on the automatic metric. Because no training stage sees a drug name, the entire evaluation is out-of-domain, so the gains reflect learned pronunciation rather than memorization. In a blinded, randomized human study, adult listeners judge 84% of our clips correct, versus 82% for the strongest baseline, with overlapping confidence intervals on a stratified subset. Across all 250 matched clips, Gemini agrees with the human majority on 84.8% of binary labels (k{appa}=0.57).

papers.title: TRACE: Trustworthy Reasoning from Acoustic Cues and Evidence
papers.abstract: We introduce TRACE (Trustworthy Reasoning from Acoustic Cues and Evidence), a benchmark for diagnosing the reliability of large audio-language models (LALMs) by revealing when, and under what acoustic conditions these models behave untrustworthily. Existing benchmarks primarily measure whether a model produces the correct answer, but correctness alone cannot determine whether the answer is grounded in acoustic evidence or instead reflects language and contextual priors. TRACE evaluates model behavior along three complementary dimensions: (1) task performance, whether the answer is correct; (2) evidence alignment, whether the model is attending to the audio regions required to answer the question; and (3) robustness, whether answers and attributed evidence respond coherently to controlled changes such as event order, overlap, signal-to-noise ratio, or background content. TRACE targets temporal ordering, counting, and event existence, three tasks that remain challenging for current models. We synthesize contextually informed acoustic scenes that allow us to test whether models hallucinate events associated with the context but absent from the audio. This synthesis also allows us to obtain a scalable benchmark for which we know the answers by design. For each scene, we create controlled variants in a programmatic way to stress-test model robustness. We introduce attribution-based metrics that quantify model attention at scale on target events and non-target events. Evaluation across five state-of-the-art models shows that current LALMs often detect where relevant sound evidence occurs, but they do not reliably interpret it, integrate it into the answer, or respond to controlled changes in that evidence. Our benchmark also shows that models still struggle the most with ordering and counting questions.

papers.title: Media Intelligence Platform: Multimodal Detection of Synthetic and Manipulated Content
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence has led to a significant increase in manipulated multimedia content, including synthetic faces, forged videos, AI-generated images, fake audio, and locally edited images. Existing detection approaches are typically designed for a single manipulation type, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios involving heterogeneous media sources. In this work, we present the Media Intelligence Platform (MIP), a unified web-based framework for multimodal media forensics integrating specialized modules for fake video detection, face morphing detection, AI-generated image detection, audio deepfake detection, localized image manipulation detection, and text analysis. Its modular architecture enables flexible integration of heterogeneous models and supports future extensions for emerging manipulation techniques. Experimental results on representative benchmark datasets demonstrate reliable detection performance across multiple media modalities while providing a practical and user-friendly interface for forensic investigations. The platform highlights the potential of unified multimodal systems for comprehensive deepfake detection in real-world environments, and is accompanied by a public demonstrator released with this workshop submission to support reproducibility and community evaluation.

models.card_text: --- inference: true tags: - musicgen - audiocraft library_name: transformers license: cc-by-nc-4.0 --- # MusicGen - Stereo - Large - 3.3B We further release a set of stereophonic capable models. Those were fine tuned for 200k updates starting from the mono models. The training data is otherwise identical and capabilities and limitations are shared with the base modes. The stereo models work by getting 2 streams of tokens from the EnCodec model, and interleaving those using the delay pattern. Stereophonic sound, also known as stereo, is a technique used to reproduce sound with depth and direction. It uses two separate audio channels played through speakers (or headphones), which creates the impression of sound coming from multiple directions. MusicGen is a text-to-music model capable of genreating high-quality music samples conditioned on text descriptions or audio prompts. It is a single stage auto-regressive Transformer model trained over a 32kHz EnCodec tokenizer with 4 codebooks sampled at 50 Hz. Unlike existing methods, like MusicLM, MusicGen doesn't require a self-supervised semantic representation, and it generates all 4 codebooks in one pass. By introducing a small delay between the codebooks, we show we can predict them in parallel, thus having only 50 auto-regressive steps per second of audio. MusicGen was published in [Simple and Controllable Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05284) by *Jade Copet, Felix Kreuk, Itai Gat, Tal Remez, David Kant, Gabriel Synnaeve, Yossi Adi, Alexandre Défossez*. We provide a simple API and 10 pre-trained models. The pre trained models are: - `facebook/musicgen-small`: 300M model, text to music only - [🤗 Hub](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-small) - `facebook/musicgen-medium`: 1.5B model, text to music only - [🤗 Hub](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-medium) - `facebook/musicgen-melody`: 1.5B model, text to music and text+melody to music - [🤗 Hub](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-melody) - `facebook/musicgen-large`: 3.3B model, text to music only - [🤗 Hub](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-large) - `facebook/musicgen-melody-large`: 3.3B model, text to music and text+melody to music - [🤗 Hub](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-melody-large) - `facebook/musicgen-stereo-*`: All the previous models fine-tuned for stereo generation - [small](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-stereo-small), [medium](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-stereo-medium), [large](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-stereo-large), [melody](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-stereo-melody), [melody large](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-stereo-melody-large) ## Example Try out MusicGen yourself! * Audiocraft Colab: * Hugging Face Colab: * Hugging Face Demo: ## 🤗 Transformers Usage You can run MusicGen Stereo models locally with the 🤗 Transformers library from `main` onward. 1. First install the 🤗 [Transformers library](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers) and scipy: ``` pip install --upgrade pip pip install --upgrade git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git scipy ``` 2. Run inference via the `Text-to-Audio` (TTA) pipeline. You can infer the MusicGen model via the TTA pipeline in just a few lines of code! ```python import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import pipeline synthesiser = pipeline("text-to-audio", "facebook/musicgen-stereo-small", device="cuda:0", torch_dtype=torch.float16) music = synthesiser("lo-fi music with a soothing melody", forward_params={"max_new_tokens": 256}) sf.write("musicgen_out.wav", music["audio"][0].T, music["sampling_rate"]) ``` 3. Run inference via the Transformers modelling code. You can use the processor + generate code to convert text into a mono 32 kHz audio waveform for more fine-grained control. ```python from transformers import AutoProcessor, MusicgenForConditionalGeneration processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("facebook/musicgen-stereo-large") model = MusicgenForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("facebook/musicgen-stereo-large").to("cuda") inputs = processor( text=["80s pop track with bassy drums and synth", "90s rock song with loud guitars and heavy drums"], padding=True, return_tensors="pt", ).to("cuda") audio_values = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256) ``` 4. Listen to the audio samples either in an ipynb notebook: ```python from IPython.display import Audio sampling_rate = model.config.audio_encoder.sampling_rate Audio(audio_values[0].cpu().numpy(), rate=sampling_rate) ``` Or save them as a `.wav` file using a third-party library, e.g. `soundfile`: ```python import soundfile as sf sampling_rate = model.config.audio_encoder.sampling_rate audio_values = audio_values.cpu().numpy() sf.write("musicgen_out.wav", audio_values[0].T, sampling_rate) ``` For more details on using the MusicGen model for inference using the 🤗 Transformers library, refer to the [MusicGen docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/musicgen). ## Audiocraft Usage You can also run MusicGen locally through the original [Audiocraft library]((https://github.com/facebookresearch/audiocraft): 1. First install the [`audiocraft` library](https://github.com/facebookresearch/audiocraft) ``` pip install git+https://github.com/facebookresearch/audiocraft.git ``` 2. Make sure to have [`ffmpeg`](https://ffmpeg.org/download.html) installed: ``` apt get install ffmpeg ``` 3. Run the following Python code: ```py from audiocraft.models import MusicGen from audiocraft.data.audio import audio_write model = MusicGen.get_pretrained("large") model.set_generation_params(duration=8) # generate 8 seconds. descriptions = ["happy rock", "energetic EDM"] wav = model.generate(descriptions) # generates 2 samples. for idx, one_wav in enumerate(wav): # Will save under {idx}.wav, with loudness normalization at -14 db LUFS. audio_write(f'{idx}', one_wav.cpu(), model.sample_rate, strategy="loudness") ``` ## Model details **Organization developing the model:** The FAIR team of Meta AI. **Model date:** MusicGen was trained between April 2023 and May 2023. **Model version:** This is the version 1 of the model. **Model type:** MusicGen consists of an EnCodec model for audio tokenization, an auto-regressive language model based on the transformer architecture for music modeling. The model comes in different sizes: 300M, 1.5B and 3.3B parameters ; and two variants: a model trained for text-to-music generation task and a model trained for melody-guided music generation. **Paper or resources for more information:** More information can be found in the paper [Simple and Controllable Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05284). **Citation details:** ``` @misc{copet2023simple, title={Simple and Controllable Music Generation}, author={Jade Copet and Felix Kreuk and Itai Gat and Tal Remez and David Kant and Gabriel Synnaeve and Yossi Adi and Alexandre Défossez}, year={2023}, eprint={2306.05284}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.SD} } ``` **License:** Code is released under MIT, model weights are released under CC-BY-NC 4.0. **Where to send questions or comments about the model:** Questions and comments about MusicGen can be sent via the [Github repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/audiocraft) of the project, or by opening an issue. ## Intended use **Primary intended use:** The primary use of MusicGen is research on AI-based music generation, including: - Research efforts, such as probing and better understanding the limitations of generative models to further improve the state of science - Generation of music guided by text or melody to understand current abilities of generative AI models by machine learning amateurs **Primary intended users:** The primary intended users of the model are researchers in audio, machine learning and artificial intelligence, as well as amateur seeking to better understand those models. **Out-of-scope use cases:** The model should not be used on downstream applications without further risk evaluation and mitigation. The model should not be used to intentionally create or disseminate music pieces that create hostile or alienating environments for people. This includes generating music that people would foreseeably find disturbing, distressing, or offensive; or content that propagates historical or current stereotypes. ## Metrics **Models performance measures:** We used the following objective measure to evaluate the model on a standard music benchmark: - Frechet Audio Distance computed on features extracted from a pre-trained audio classifier (VGGish) - Kullback-Leibler Divergence on label distributions extracted from a pre-trained audio classifier (PaSST) - CLAP Score between audio embedding and text embedding extracted from a pre-trained CLAP model Additionally, we run qualitative studies with human participants, evaluating the performance of the model with the following axes: - Overall quality of the music samples; - Text relevance to the provided text input; - Adherence to the melody for melody-guided music generation. More details on performance measures and human studies can be found in the paper. **Decision thresholds:** Not applicable. ## Evaluation datasets The model was evaluated on the [MusicCaps benchmark](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/googleai/musiccaps) and on an in-domain held-out evaluation set, with no artist overlap with the training set. ## Training datasets The model was trained on licensed data using the following sources: the [Meta Music Initiative Sound Collection](https://www.fb.com/sound), [Shutterstock music collection](https://www.shutterstock.com/music) and the [Pond5 music collection](https://www.pond5.com/). See the paper for more details about the training set and corresponding preprocessing. ## Evaluation results Below are the objective metrics obtained on MusicCaps with the released model. Note that for the publicly released models, we had all the datasets go through a state-of-the-art music source separation method, namely using the open source [Hybrid Transformer for Music Source Separation](https://github.com/facebookresearch/demucs) (HT-Demucs), in order to keep only the instrumental part. This explains the difference in objective metrics with the models used in the paper. | Model | Frechet Audio Distance | KLD | Text Consistency | Chroma Cosine Similarity | |---|---|---|---|---| | facebook/musicgen-small | 4.88 | 1.42 | 0.27 | - | | facebook/musicgen-medium | 5.14 | 1.38 | 0.28 | - | | **facebook/musicgen-large** | 5.48 | 1.37 | 0.28 | - | | facebook/musicgen-melody | 4.93 | 1.41 | 0.27 | 0.44 | More information can be found in the paper [Simple and Controllable Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05284), in the Results section. ## Limitations and biases **Data:** The data sources used to train the model are created by music professionals and covered by legal agreements with the right holders. The model is trained on 20K hours of data, we believe that scaling the model on larger datasets can further improve the performance of the model. **Mitigations:** Vocals have been removed from the data source using corresponding tags, and then using a state-of-the-art music source separation method, namely using the open source [Hybrid Transformer for Music Source Separation](https://github.com/facebookresearch/demucs) (HT-Demucs). **Limitations:** - The model is not able to generate realistic vocals. - The model has been trained with English descriptions and will not perform as well in other languages. - The model does not perform equally well for all music styles and cultures. - The model sometimes generates end of songs, collapsing to silence. - It is sometimes difficult to assess what types of text descriptions provide the best generations. Prompt engineering may be required to obtain satisfying results. **Biases:** The source of data is potentially lacking diversity and all music cultures are not equally represented in the dataset. The model may not perform equally well on the wide variety of music genres that exists. The generated samples from the model will reflect the biases from the training data. Further work on this model should include methods for balanced and just representations of cultures, for example, by scaling the training data to be both diverse and inclusive. **Risks and harms:** Biases and limitations of the model may lead to generation of samples that may be considered as biased, inappropriate or offensive. We believe that providing the code to reproduce the research and train new models will allow to broaden the application to new and more representative data. **Use cases:** Users must be aware of the biases, limitations and risks of the model. # MuLaCover — Cover Song & Music Remix Generation

MuLaCover is a controllable AI cover-song and music-remix model. It transforms
reference music using lyrics and a structured text style prompt, or generates
from melody/chord MIDI. The standalone inference code is maintained in the
[MuLaCover repository](https://github.com/HeartMuLa/MuLaCover).

[HeartMuLa repository](https://github.com/HeartMuLa/heartlib) ·
[HeartMuLa paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10547)

> Model weights are publicly available for download. No access request is required.

## Inputs

Lyrics use section markers and preserved line breaks:

```text
[Verse]
One lyric line
Another lyric line

[Chorus]
One chorus line
```

Style is one UTF-8 line using named fields:

```text
topic:[Longing]; genre:[country]; instrument:[Strings,acoustic guitar]; mood:[hopeful]
```

## Download

Download the model weights with the Hugging Face CLI. Authentication is not required:

```bash
hf download HeartMuLa/MuLaCover --local-dir ./ckpt/MuLaCover
```

Also download HeartCodec and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
into sibling checkpoint directories. Reference-audio conditioning also needs
the documented YourMT3 and ChordNet checkpoints. See the code repository for
the complete installation and generation commands.

## Usage

Install the `mulacover` package and prepare all checkpoint directories using
the [generation guide](https://github.com/HeartMuLa/MuLaCover/blob/main/examples/cover_song_generation.md).
Run the following from the code repository root. `./ckpt` is the parent
directory containing MuLaCover, HeartCodec, Qwen3, and the transcription models.

```python
import torch
from mulacover import MuLaCoverGenPipeline

torch.manual_seed(42)
pipe = MuLaCoverGenPipeline.from_pretrained(
    "./ckpt",
    device=torch.device("cuda:0"),
    dtype={
        "mulacover": torch.bfloat16,
        "codec": torch.float32,
        "qwen": torch.float32,
        "transcriptor": torch.float32,
    },
    lazy_load=True,
)
pipe(
    {
        "ref_audio": "/path/to/reference.mp3",
        "lyrics": "assets/lyrics.txt",
        "tags": "assets/tags.txt",
    },
    save_path="cover.wav",
)
```

The pipeline writes a WAV file. Use the MuLaCover package API shown above;
this model is not a built-in Transformers model class.

- `config.json`: MuLaCover model architecture configuration.
- `gen_config.json`: audio/text token identifiers used during generation.
- `model-00001-of-00005.safetensors` … `model-00005-of-00005.safetensors`:
  sharded model weights.
- `model.safetensors.index.json`: shard index.
- `tokenizer.json`: lyrics and prompt tokenizer.

# RubatoCodec

[![Code: GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/Code-GitHub-black?logo=github)](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec)
![Paper: coming soon](https://img.shields.io/badge/Paper-coming%20soon-lightgrey)
[![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue)](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)

RubatoCodec is a neural speech codec that divides speech into a fixed number of
variable-duration events. Each event carries discrete code indices and an
explicit duration. Event placement adapts to speech content, while the number of
events is determined exactly by the utterance length, so the token sequence
length a speech generator must produce is predictable. A causal decoder renders
completed events incrementally, which makes the codec suitable for streaming
text-to-speech.

The name comes from the musical term *rubato*: local timing flexes while the
overall tempo is preserved.

- **Adaptive Firing with an exact event budget.** Multi-scale latent
  dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux guide cumulative allocation on a
  50-Hz latent grid. For `T` frames the event count is exactly
  `max(1, min(T, round(0.25 · T)))`, giving 12.5 events/s. No learned boundary
  predictor, boundary labels, or rate loss is used.
- **Streaming decoding.** Events can be decoded one at a time or in chunks.
  Event-by-event decoding takes about 11 ms per event on an NVIDIA H200, well
  below the ~80 ms of audio each event represents on average.
- **Hybrid residual quantizer with depth control.** A semantically supervised
  FSQ first layer is followed by 15 DAC-style residual VQ layers, each with
  4,096 entries. Any prefix depth from 1 to 16 can be decoded, giving code-index
  bitrates of 0.15–2.4 kbit/s plus duration information.
- **Multilingual.** Trained on approximately 375,000 hours of speech, mostly
  English, Japanese, and Chinese, with 16-kHz input and 44.1-kHz output.

![RubatoCodec architecture](assets/architecture.png)

## Model details

| | |
|---|---|
| Input / output sample rate | 16 kHz / 44.1 kHz |
| Latent grid | 50 Hz |
| Event rate | 12.5 events/s (retention ratio 0.25) |
| Quantizer | 16 layers × 4,096 entries; layer 0 FSQ with semantic distillation, layers 1–15 residual VQ |
| Bitrate | 1.23 kbit/s at depth 8, 2.43 kbit/s at depth 16 (LibriSpeech, including duration information) |
| Decoder | Fully causal Transformer + ISTFT head, streaming capable |
| Parameters | 246M codec (72M encoder, 173M decoder, 1M quantizer) + frozen [w2v-BERT 2.0](https://huggingface.co/facebook/w2v-bert-2.0) (580M, encoding only) |
| License | Apache 2.0 |

## Usage

Install the package from the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec
cd RubatoCodec
uv sync
```

Encode and decode:

```python
import soundfile as sf
import torch

from rubatocodec import RubatoCodec

codec = RubatoCodec.from_pretrained("third-intelligence/RubatoCodec", device="cuda")

data, sr = sf.read("speech.wav", dtype="float32")  # mono waveform
wav = torch.from_numpy(data)

enc = codec.encode(wav, sr=sr)       # {"codes": (16, K) int64, "durs": (K,) int64}
audio = codec.decode(enc)            # (1, 1, T_audio) at 44.1 kHz, full depth
audio = codec.decode(enc, depth=8)   # lower bitrate with the first 8 layers

sf.write("recon.wav", audio[0, 0].cpu().numpy(), codec.output_sr)
```

`durs` gives each event's duration in 20-ms grid frames. Loading also downloads
`facebook/w2v-bert-2.0`, which is used only for encoding.

Streaming decoding, inference settings, the code format, and training are
documented in the repository:
[inference guide](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/inference.md),
[architecture](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/architecture.md),
[training](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/training.md).

## Evaluation

RubatoCodec is evaluated on LibriSpeech test-clean, VCTK, JVS nonpara30, JVNV,
and seed-tts-eval test-zh against 13 other codecs. At comparable bitrates, it
shows the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the
English and Japanese benchmarks and high predicted quality, while the strongest
comparators achieve higher PESQ-WB and STOI.

dWER/dCER compare ASR transcripts of the reconstructed and original audio
(Whisper-large-v3 for English and Japanese, Paraformer-zh for Mandarin). SIM is
ECAPA-TDNN speaker similarity. Bitrates include duration information.

**Adaptive event placement.** Each rectangle in the lower strip is one event.

The full protocol, all compared codecs and operating points, and throughput
measurements are in the
[evaluation document](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/evaluation.md)
and the paper.

## Training data

Approximately 375,000 hours of public and internal speech. Public sources include
[Emilia-YODAS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset),
[HiFiTTS-2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/hifitts-2) (44-kHz subset),
[ReazonSpeech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/reazon-research/reazonspeech),
[The People's Speech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLCommons/peoples_speech)
(excluding ShareAlike-licensed data),
[VoxPopuli](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/voxpopuli),
[Multilingual LibriSpeech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/multilingual_librispeech)
(excluding English),
[Omnilingual ASR Corpus](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/omnilingual-asr-corpus),
and [IndicVoices](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4bharat/IndicVoices). English, Japanese,
and Chinese account for approximately 44%, 27%, and 13% of the data, and other
languages for the remaining 16%.

## Limitations

- RubatoCodec is trained on speech only and is intended for speech. It is not
  designed for music or general audio.
- Encoding requires the whole utterance, because the event budget is defined at
  the utterance level. Only decoding is streaming.
- Signal-fidelity metrics (PESQ-WB, STOI) are below those of the strongest
  compared codecs at similar bitrates.
- Evaluation covers English, Japanese, and Mandarin, all of which appear in the
  training data. Performance on other languages has not been evaluated.
- Like other speech codecs, RubatoCodec can be used in speech generation systems
  capable of voice cloning. Do not use it to impersonate people or to create
  deceptive content without consent.

## Acknowledgements

RubatoCodec builds on [X-Codec-2.0](https://github.com/zhenye234/X-Codec-2.0)
and uses [w2v-BERT 2.0](https://huggingface.co/facebook/w2v-bert-2.0) as its
frozen semantic encoder. It also adapts components from
[BigCodec](https://github.com/Aria-K-Alethia/BigCodec),
[DAC](https://github.com/descriptinc/descript-audio-codec),
[Inworld TTS](https://github.com/inworld-ai/tts), and
[BigVGAN](https://github.com/NVIDIA/BigVGAN). See the repository for the full
list and their licenses.

# DuplexJev-4B-Para (v1.2)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Release note: [why the 4B could not hear Japanese, and the fix](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-weak-languages.md)

**The small DuplexJev that hears the most beyond the words, now also in Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese and Thai.**

> **v1.2 (2026-10-21)** replaces v1.1 (2026-10-10). Earlier versions stay available as revisions `v1.1` and `v1.0`
> (`--revision v1.1` in vLLM, `revision="v1.1"` in `from_pretrained`).

v1.1 understood speech in only a handful of languages: Japanese and Korean transcription error was around 60 %, although
the frozen Qwen3-ASR encoder handles them at 3–7 %. The alignment data simply had almost no Japanese (0.05 %) and no
Korean at all. v1.2 adds that data, plus new Mandarin paralinguistic data, on top of v1.1, and keeps the rest of the
model where it was: 1,035-item paralinguistic benchmark 47.6 (v1.1 47.8), basic decisions unchanged.

Architecture: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder + connector + Qwen3-4B, 4.2 B parameters, bf16, ~10 GB GPU memory.

## What changed

Continued from v1.1: connector + a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here), 2,500 steps, the full v1.1 mix replayed
(non-verbal ×1.3, stress ×1.2), plus:

| added data | items | what it teaches |
|---|---:|---|
| weak-language speech (ja, ko, vi, th, ar, ru): Emilia, Emilia-YODAS, YODAS2, Zeroth-Korean, VIVOS, FLEURS train, Common Voice | 162 k | transcribe; every label re-checked against Qwen3-ASR-0.6B, disagreeing clips dropped |
| continuation in the same six languages (text teacher: Qwen3-32B) | 36 k | understand, not just repeat |
| Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (licensed MagicData corpus, training speakers only) | 18 k | laughter, laughing while talking, breath, lip smack, sniff, cough, stressed word, drawl, sentence emotion |

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para --max-model-len 4096
# previous version: add --revision v1.1
```

Decision prompts are the same as for [DuplexJev-4B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Turn); see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions. For
conversation, send the user audio as the user turn (`<|audio|>`) with ordinary chat history and sample as usual.

## Limitations

- Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese and Thai are much better but still 3–6× the encoder's own error; Arabic improved least
  (little everyday Arabic speech in the new data). The 32B models are stronger in these languages.
- Spoken qa100 is 3 points and StressPresso 4.5 points below v1.1; MSPB is 2.4 points lower.
- Asked about itself, it may describe abilities (seeing images, speaking) that this checkpoint does not have on its own:
  it takes speech and text and replies in text.
- Speaker judgments are coarse and must not be used to identify or verify people; emotion outputs must not be used to
  make decisions about individuals.

# Chatterbox Amharic

A LoRA adapter and an extended Fidel tokenizer that teach
[Chatterbox Multilingual v3](https://huggingface.co/ResembleAI/chatterbox)
(Resemble AI, MIT) to speak Amharic, with voice cloning from about ten
seconds of reference audio. Trained only on speech we own or that is licensed
for it.

Stock Chatterbox cannot read Amharic at all: its tokenizer maps every Ge'ez
character to `[UNK]`. So the "before" clips below aren't a weaker version of
the same thing; they're the model guessing at unknown tokens. We add 244
tokens for the script and teach the model what they sound like.

The repo also has [`amharic_text.py`](amharic_text.py), the text normalizer
the model was trained through. No dependencies, works on its own
([below](#amharic-text-front-end)).

## Hear it

Each pair uses the same sentence, reference audio, settings and seed. No
language tag on either: the adapter was trained without one, and the stock
tokenizer has no Ge'ez characters.

`amharic_text.normalize`, `temperature=0.6`, `cfg_weight=0.5`, seed 1234.
One take per sentence per model, no picking. Known weaknesses are under

## What this is, and what it isn't

An adapter: LoRA weights on the T3 text-to-speech-token transformer,
full-rank embeddings for the new tokens, and the extended tokenizer. You
apply it on top of Chatterbox Multilingual v3, which you download from
Resemble. We ship our delta, not a copy of their model.

Not merged weights, not a standalone model. Amharic only: Tigrinya and Ge'ez
use the same script, but the adapter was not trained on them.

## Amharic text front-end

[`amharic_text.py`](amharic_text.py) built the training labels, and the
loader runs it on every input, so training and inference see the same text.
One file, standard library only, same licence as the adapter, usable
without the model. (One fix since training: a dotted abbreviation's trailing
dot mid-sentence, as in `… ዓ.ም. የአገሪቱ …`, is no longer read as a full stop.
Labels were built with the version whose SHA-256 is in
`training_config.json`; the only effect on the model is one fewer spurious
pause.)

It converts Ge'ez numerals, digits, decimals, percentages and clock times to
words (`1500` → አንድ ሺህ አምስት መቶ, `75%` → ሰባ አምስት በመቶ, `3:30` → ሶስት ሰዓት
ተኩል); expands about a hundred common abbreviations, keeping the inflected
suffix (`ዶ/ር` → ዶክተር, `ዓ.ም.` → ዓመተ ምሕረት, `መ/ቤቱ` → መሥሪያ ቤቱ); collapses the
four consonant families that are spelled several ways but pronounced the same
(ሐ ኀ ኅ → ሀ, ሠ → ሰ, ዐ → አ, ፀ → ጸ); reduces punctuation to the five marks that
change how you say something (`።` `፣` `፤` `?` `!`); strips URLs, emoji and
control characters. It's a subset of what we run in production.

```python
from amharic_text import normalize, split_sentences
normalize("ዶ/ር አበበ በ2018 ዓ.ም በተደረገው ምርጫ 75% ድምፅ አገኙ።")
# 'ዶክተር አበበ በሁለት ሺህ አስራ ስምንት ኣመተ ምህረት በተደረገው ምርጫ ሰባ አምስት በመቶ ድምጽ አገኙ።'
```

## Training data

Three sources. Every clip's filename starts with its corpus prefix; the
assembled training directory was audited before training and the output is
committed as is ([`audit/corpus_audit.txt`](audit/corpus_audit.txt)). The
adapter was trained from scratch on exactly that directory, starting from
Resemble's stock v3 T3.

| prefix | source | licence | clips | hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ih_` | Our own studio recordings | ours | 573 | 1.25 |
| `wxl_` | [WaxalNLP](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/WaxalNLP) Amharic (Digital Umuganda / Google) | CC-BY-SA-4.0 | 40921 | 190.93 |
| `cv_` | [Common Voice](https://commonvoice.mozilla.org/) Amharic | CC0-1.0 | 1055 | 1.45 |
| | **total** | | 42549 | 193.63 |

WaxalNLP comes as 48 kHz and Common Voice as 32/48 kHz MP3; both were
resampled to 24 kHz. All Waxal Amharic clips that fit the trainer's 3 to 25
second window were used (190.93 h of roughly 191).

## Licence: why CC-BY-SA-4.0

WaxalNLP is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, so the adapter is released under CC
BY-SA 4.0. Credit to Digital Umuganda, the WaxalNLP contributors, and the
Common Voice contributors. The base model is MIT; this licence covers what we
add.

## Architecture

Base: Chatterbox Multilingual v3, `ResembleAI/chatterbox` at revision
`5bb1f6ee58e50c3b8d408bc82a6d3740c2db6e18`, T3 file `t3_mtl23ls_v3.safetensors`. Pinned on purpose:
the adapter only makes sense on that exact T3. v3 has Resemble's
hallucination and speaker-similarity fixes over v2; S3Gen, the voice encoder
and the tokenizer are the same as v2 and untouched.

| component | treatment |
|---|---|
| T3 (text→speech-token transformer, 0.5 B) | LoRA r=64, α=128, dropout 0.05 on `q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj` + `spkr_enc`; base weights frozen |
| `text_emb` / `text_head` | trained full-rank and shipped whole (PEFT `modules_to_save`). New vocabulary rows can't be learned through a low-rank delta. |
| Tokenizer | base multilingual tokenizer + 244 added tokens: every Ge'ez character seen in the corpus, plus ። ፣ ፤ ? ! and U+135F. `"ሰላም"` in the stock tokenizer is `[UNK] [UNK] [UNK]`. |
| S3Gen (speech tokens → waveform, includes the PerTh watermark) | frozen, not shipped |
| Voice encoder | frozen, not shipped |

Notes for anyone building on this:

*No language token.* The base tokenizer has `[fr]`, `[de]` and so on; there
is no `[am]` and we didn't add one. The adapter was trained on plain
normalized text, and the loader tokenizes without a language prefix, without
lower-casing or NFKD. `language_id="am"` on stock
`ChatterboxMultilingualTTS.generate` raises `ValueError`; use the loader.

*Alignment guard is off.* Upstream enables its attention-alignment
hallucination guard only when `text_tokens_dict_size == 2454`. With the
extended vocabulary it's off, in training and at inference. The loader chunks
by sentence instead, which handles the common failure (T3 stopping at the
first sentence-final mark).

*Train/inference parity.* The shipped `amharic_text.py` differs from the file
that built the training labels by later punctuation fixes. Both hashes and the
reason are recorded in [`training_config.json`](training_config.json) as
`label_frontend_sha256`, `label_frontend_sha256_shipped` and
`label_frontend_changed_since_training`. Property checks over every training
transcript are in [`audit/frontend_check.txt`](audit/frontend_check.txt).

## Evaluation

Held-out set: 100 clips from the same corpus, split before training
by a seeded speaker-disjoint rule, so whole speakers are held out and none of
their sentences appear in training. Checked independently of the trainer's
own assertion: HELD OUT: eval ∩ train = ∅ at clip, speaker and sentence level; all eval stems are ih_/wxl_/cv_.
([`audit/holdout_verify.txt`](audit/holdout_verify.txt)). Both models ran on
the same clips with the same per-clip reference audio (the held-out
speaker's own recording), through the same code: the released loader for the
adapter, stock v3 with the same normalized text and no language tag.

| metric | stock Chatterbox v3 | + Gabar adapter |
|---|---|---|
| Amharic CER ↓ (Meta omniASR-CTC-3B) | 0.932 | 0.095 |
| UTMOS ↑ (naturalness MOS predictor) | 2.359 | 2.711 |
| ECAPA cosine ↑ (speaker similarity to reference) | 0.610 | 0.860 |
| generation failures (empty / <0.5 s / error) | 0.0% | 1.0% |

Per-clip numbers: [`audit/eval/`](audit/eval/).

How CER is measured. We transcribe the generated audio with Meta's stock
[omniASR-CTC-3B](https://huggingface.co/facebook/omniASR-CTC-3B), which we
didn't train, and compare to the reference text after `normalize_for_metric`
(collapses the homophone families so ሀ/ሐ/ኀ spellings don't count as errors,
strips punctuation). Same ASR, same normalization, both models. The stock
column is a floor: the base model can't read Fidel, so most of what it
produces isn't Amharic. UTMOS and ECAPA involve no ASR. UTMOS was trained on
English MOS ratings and both outputs are Amharic, so its near-tie says more
about the metric than the models. Means are over clips that produced audio;
failures are on their own row so they can't hide in an average.

Our own listening verdict: intelligible Amharic, not yet fully natural
(read-aloud cadence, occasional flat prosody); the stock output is garbled and
not Amharic.

## Usage

```bash
pip install "chatterbox-tts @ git+https://github.com/resemble-ai/chatterbox@5de7a54aa4e5e2baadb0182dde554908b48b85c2" peft safetensors huggingface_hub torchaudio
```

```python
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
import importlib.util, torchaudio

# the loader + text front-end ship in this repo
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
    "amharic_tts", hf_hub_download("gabar-tech/chatterbox-amharic", "amharic_tts.py"))
amharic_tts = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(amharic_tts)

tts = amharic_tts.load_amharic_tts(device="cuda")   # downloads base v3 (pinned) + adapter
wav = tts.generate(
    "ሰላም! ይህ ከጽሑፍ በቀጥታ የተፈጠረ የአማርኛ ድምፅ ነው። ዛሬ ነሐሴ 11 ቀን 2018 ዓ.ም. ነው።",
    audio_prompt_path="reference.wav",     # ~10 s of the voice to clone, with consent
    temperature=0.6, cfg_weight=0.5)
torchaudio.save("out.wav", wav, tts.sr)      # 24 kHz, PerTh-watermarked
print(tts.normalize("ዛሬ ነሐሴ 11 ቀን 2018 ዓ.ም. ነው።"))   # what the model actually read
```

Or from a checkout: `python amharic_tts.py "ሰላም ዓለም።" --ref reference.wav --out out.wav`.

`generate()` normalizes the text, splits at sentence-final marks (T3 tends to
stop at the first ። / ? / !), synthesizes each sentence against the
reference and joins them. `normalize=False` / `split_sentences=False` turn
those off. We ran the snippet above as written in a fresh virtualenv with
only the packages listed, on NVIDIA RTX A6000, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, python 3.11.10, torch 2.6.0+cu124, chatterbox-tts@5de7a54, peft 0.20.0, before publishing.

## Watermarking

Chatterbox puts Resemble's PerTh watermark in every waveform it generates.
We left that alone; nothing in this adapter touches S3Gen or the vocoder,
where it happens. We ran the public `resemble-perth` detector over every demo
clip from both models and the held-out eval outputs, with the natural
reference recording as a negative control: present on all 115 checked files (detector confidence ≥ 0.5 on every generated file; the natural reference recording scores 0.0, so the detector is discriminating)
([`audit/watermark_verify.txt`](audit/watermark_verify.txt)). If you build on
this, leave it in. It's about the only provenance signal that exists for
synthetic Amharic right now.

## Intended use

- Amharic speech interfaces, audiobooks, education, accessibility, media
  production, with the consent of whoever's voice you clone.
- Research on low-resource TTS, script extension, Ethiopian language tech.

## Out of scope

- Cloning someone's voice without their informed consent.
- Political persuasion, impersonating public figures, fraud (voice
  authentication included), harassment.
- Other languages. The adapter makes the base worse at its other languages.
- Anything safety-critical or broadcast without a human listening first.

## Limitations

- Gemination (consonant length; contrastive in Amharic, unwritten in normal
  spelling) isn't marked. The model reads minimal pairs like አለ "said" / አለ
  "there is" from context and will get some wrong. Our internal models use a
  lexicon-based marker; we left it out so that what you type is what the
  model was trained on, with nothing private in between.
- Numbers, abbreviations and Ge'ez numerals are expanded by
  `amharic_text.py`. Skip it, or feed it things it doesn't handle (currency
  symbols, odd date formats, Latin words), and the model gets them raw.
- The first word or two of an utterance are sometimes slurred before the
  model settles; mid-sentence text is steadier. Sentences that open with a
  number phrase show it most.
- Ejectives (ቀ, ጠ, ጨ, ጰ, ጸ) are much better than nothing but not uniformly
  native.
- Very short inputs (a single word, "እሺ") can come out unstable. Put them in
  a sentence.
- Long passages: chunk at sentence boundaries. The loader does this for you.
- 193.63 hours, most of it read speech (Waxal and Common Voice are
  ASR corpora). Expect a neutral, read-aloud delivery; expressive and
  spontaneous speech is thin.
- Amharic only.

## Risks and misuse

This model can clone a voice from roughly ten seconds of reference audio, so
it can be misused for impersonation or fraud. Use it only with informed
consent and human review. Outputs are watermarked by the shipped inference
path. Every voice in the training data was recorded under a licence that
permits this use.

  (CC-BY-SA-4.0).
- Mozilla Common Voice contributors, Amharic speech data (CC0-1.0).

# Drama-3 int4 KoEn160 (Korean/English expert-pruned, based on Fish Audio Drama 3)

**Built with Fish Audio.** An unofficial Korean/English variant of
[fishaudio/drama-3-int4](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3-int4), made to run on a single
24 GB GPU (RTX 3090). Not endorsed by Fish Audio.

- **Runs within 24 GB of VRAM.**
- **3–4× faster than the cloud server.**

## What changed

| | fishaudio/drama-3-int4 | this model |
|---|---|---|
| Routed experts per MoE layer | 256 | **160** (Korean/English) |
| Weights on disk | 23 GB | 17 GB |
| lm_head · embed_tokens · audio decoder linears | bf16 | bf16 on disk, **Hadamard int8 at load** with the patch below |

- **Expert pruning.** We ran the original model on about 150 Korean and English lines, counted which
  routed experts the router picked in each layer, and kept the 160 most used. No retraining.
  Languages other than Korean and English were not kept in mind and are likely worse.
- **Hadamard 8-bit (optional, runtime).** `sglang-omni-patch/drama3-hadamard8.patch` makes
  SGLang-Omni rotate each 256-wide group with a Hadamard matrix and store the remaining bf16
  layers as int8 (W8A8) while loading, saving about 1.9 GB of GPU memory (relative error 1.2–1.5 %).

## Measured (RTX 3090 24 GB, Hadamard 8-bit on)

- Server ready in 54 s; one line synthesised at **3.1–3.3× real time** (original int4 on the same
  card, with the codec on CPU to fit: about 0.9×).
- Peak GPU memory 23.4 GB.
- Settings we used: engine memory fraction 0.58, vocoder 0.18, reference reading 4096 MiB,
  at most 560 frames (≈26 s) per line, vocoder CUDA graph off, reference encoder and vocoder in fp32 on GPU.

## Run with SGLang-Omni


# Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-MNN

[Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B) converted to
[MNN](https://github.com/alibaba/MNN) and quantised, for CPU inference without PyTorch
or ONNX Runtime.  44.1 kHz speech, Chinese and English, zero-shot voice cloning.

The conversion covers the whole model: the Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone (`lm`), the CFM/DiT
flow-matching head (`dit`), the `aggregator`, the audio-VAE encoder (`enc_backbone`,
`enc_agg`), the decoder/vocoder (`voc`) and the CAM++ speaker encoder (`campplus`) —
seven graphs per tier.

## One command

```bash
uvx --from ming-tts-mnn ming-tts "傍晚的风从山口吹过来，远处的云慢慢染成了金色。" -o hello.wav
```

`uvx` builds an isolated environment, installs the package, runs it, and leaves your
Python alone.  The first run also downloads the tier it needs (`-p fp16|int8|int4`)
plus the shared assets.  Or use it from Python:

```python
from ming_tts_mnn import MingTTSMNN

tts = MingTTSMNN.from_pretrained("int8")
wav = tts.synthesize("傍晚的风从山口吹过来。")           # float32, 44.1 kHz
```

With `--model-dir` / `MingTTSMNN(local_dir)` the same code runs on this repository's
files directly.

## Files

```
assets/      dims.json, host.npz (host-side tensors), embed.npy      261 MB
tokenizer/   tokenizer.json + configs                                 15 MB
fp16/        lm, dit, aggregator, enc_backbone, enc_agg, voc, campplus  2.63 GB
int8/        same seven graphs                                       1.52 GB
int4/        same seven graphs at 4 bits                             0.77 GB
samples/     reference and converted wavs for two cases
```

`assets/` and `tokenizer/` are shared by all tiers.

## How close is it to the original?

The release runs in bf16, so "the original" already has ~8 mantissa bits of rounding.
Two measurements, in increasing order of "what you hear":

**Step by step, same noise, same inputs.** The MNN fp16 graph differs from the fp32
release by 9.0e-4 (relative peak) at the first flow-matching step, growing to 2.8e-2
over eight steps.  The release's *own* bf16 run differs from its fp32 run by 2.1e-2 at
the first step and 4.1e-1 at the worst step — so MNN fp16 is 12–23× closer to the fp32
model than the shipped model is to itself.  int8 starts at 2.2e-2, i.e. on par with
the release's own bf16 rounding; int4 starts at 0.62, i.e. another numerical regime.

**End to end** (log-mel L1 / CAM++ speaker cosine, against the fp32 release with the
same noise):

| case | release bf16 | MNN fp16 | MNN int8 | MNN int4 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| a, 4 s Chinese, cloning | 10.14 dB / 0.914 | **7.91 / 0.945** | 11.33 / 0.864 | 12.46 / 0.838 |
| b, same text, zero speaker | 10.10 / 0.921 | **4.31 / 0.988** | 10.77 / 0.957 | 16.88 / 0.468 |
| d, 3-sentence paragraph, forced as one fragment | 11.45 / 0.954 | **10.49 / 0.967** | 10.99 / 0.963 | 13.83 / 0.505 |

For calibration: a different noise draw of the *original itself* scores 12.84 dB and
0.893 cosine on case a.  MNN fp16 is inside that envelope on spectrum and timbre.

Whisper-small character error rate on that forced single-fragment paragraph: release
fp32 30.0%, release bf16 32.9%, MNN fp16 27.1%, int8 31.4%, int4 80.0%.

**16 extra texts, sentence-split like the shipping CLI.**  12 sentences and 4
paragraphs, all synthesised with the same seed as fp16 and compared against it:
int8 CAM++ speaker cosine 0.932–0.996 (mean 0.979), int4 0.828–0.927 (mean 0.879).
Whisper transcribed 16/16 clips for fp16, int8 and int4; none of them looped or hit
the decode budget.  So int4's case-d failure is a long-fragment failure mode, not
what you get when the CLI splits the text — but int4's timbre is still audibly
coarser than int8 on every one of those 16 texts.

Full tables, the calibration controls and the per-graph error floors:
[FIDELITY.zh.md](FIDELITY.zh.md) (Chinese).

## Which tier should I use?

* **fp16** — the default.  2.63 GB, closest to the original in every measurement.
* **int8** — 1.52 GB, spectrum within a couple of dB of fp16, speaker cosine still
  0.93–0.996 across the 16 extra texts, long-form ASR on par with the original.  The
  best size/quality trade.
* **int4** — 0.77 GB, all 4-bit.  Every one of the 16 extra texts was transcribed and
  none looped, but timbre and articulation are noticeably coarser than int8.  A long
  paragraph forced through as a single fragment can still fall into repetition (case d
  in the table), so keep int8 unless memory is the hard limit.

## Speed

Apple M5 Pro, 4 threads, 44.1 kHz output: a 3–6 s sentence takes 1–2× its duration
(RTF 1.1–2.0).  The flow-matching head dominates the cost — ten DiT evaluations per
latent step against one LM decode — so per-step cost is the same in all three tiers.

Held at the same 40 decode steps (3.20 s of audio), the quantized tiers still finish
sooner because their one-off costs (prompt prefill, encoder, vocoder) shrink with the
weights: int8 8.9 s and int4 8.3 s against fp16's 10.1 s, with PyTorch bf16 at 21.8 s.
That is ~12% and ~18% faster than fp16 end to end, roughly half what the 4× smaller
weights would suggest, and the gap closes on long utterances.  Treat int4 as a disk
and memory saving first.

## Notes and limitations

* The release stops an utterance when a learned stop head crosses 0.5.  That decision
  is discrete and sensitive to accumulated rounding, so two runs that differ only in
  arithmetic can differ in length — including the original's own fp32 vs bf16 runs
  (45 vs 50 decode steps on the same input).  Durations in the table above should be
  read that way.
* English with the zero-speaker default voice is weak in the **original** checkpoints:
  the release itself turns the test sentence into unintelligible syllables for the
  full 26 s budget.  The conversion reproduces that behaviour rather than causing it.
  Prompt-based cloning works normally in both languages.
* With `use_zero_spk_emb` the speaker vector is exactly zero *after* projection; the
  default voice this produces varies with the noise draw (two runs of the original
  score 0.39 cosine against each other), so speaker similarity is only meaningful
  against a same-noise reference.
* This repository contains weights only; the code is in the `ming-tts-mnn` PyPI
  package.  The package also accepts `--source modelscope`.
